title: Can gas grow its role in Indian power markets?
gist: Gas has been structurally squeezed out of India's power mix over 15 years — capacity share halved from 10% to 4% and it now generates only about 1% of electricity — with Wood Mackenzie attributing this to four compounding constraints: insufficient affordable domestic gas making imported LNG the marginal price-setter, allocation rules that rank power below transport, households and fertiliser, uneven pipeline connectivity creating a two-tier fleet, and LNG costs that lose to coal and renewables-plus-battery. The piece is a gated teaser that withholds most of the quantitative answers behind a download form.

themes.theme: Structural decline of Indian gas power

insights.claim: Gas has been steadily displaced from India's power mix over the last 15 years, with its capacity share more than halving from 10% to just 4%.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: India is not a growth market for gas turbines today — treat Indian gas-to-power capex forecasts with scepticism until allocation policy changes.
insights.quote: its capacity share more than halving from 10% to just 4%
insights.locator: Over the last 15 years, gas has been steadily displaced

insights.claim: India's gas-fired plants were built for baseload but now survive mostly as peaking and flexibility resources, generating only around 1% of the country's electricity.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: The gap between 4% of capacity and 1% of generation quantifies a massive stranded-asset problem and caps the LNG offtake these plants can support.
insights.locator: The country’s gas-fired power plants were built for baseload

insights.claim: Gas-fired power is well-positioned to support increasingly variable renewable generation in India, mainly by providing flexibility during peak demand periods, but only if structural challenges are overcome.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: The bull case for Indian gas is a flexibility-value case, not a volume case — it needs capacity or ancillary-services market design to monetise.
insights.locator: Gas-fired power is well-positioned to take on a key role

insights.claim: Despite its limited role as a balancing fuel today, Indian gas-fired generation is destined to grow significantly in the 2040s.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: The Indian gas-power opportunity is a 2040s story, far beyond most investment horizons — near-term LNG demand growth must come from other sectors.
insights.locator: Despite its limited role as a balancing fuel

insights.claim: Recent upstream additions have driven a recovery in Indian gas production after more than a decade of falling supply from the large but mature KG-D6 field, yet supply remains well below demand.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Even a domestic production recovery does not close the gap — India stays structurally short and import-dependent.

insights.claim: Because India's gas shortfall is filled by imported LNG, international gas prices are the marginal driver of Indian gas-fired plant economics.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Indian gas-power dispatch is effectively a call option on JKM — Indian demand is the swing buyer that disappears when LNG spot prices spike.
insights.quote: The shortfall is made up for with imported LNG, making international gas prices the marginal driver of gas-fired plant economics.

insights.claim: Under India's Domestic Gas Allocation Policy, transport, households and fertiliser use are prioritised ahead of power generation, structurally marginalising gas-fired electricity.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Cheap domestic gas is legally out of reach for power — no amount of LNG price relief fixes the allocation problem, so watch for policy reform as the real catalyst.
insights.locator: 2. Policy: Market design and allocation rules

insights.claim: Coal remains India's preferred fuel for energy security reasons, and the absence of effective policy support limits investment in new gas-fired generation.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Energy-security politics, not economics, is the primary reason Indian coal keeps its position — a headwind for any coal-to-gas switching thesis in India.
insights.locator: 2. Policy: Market design and allocation rules

insights.claim: Uneven gas pipeline connectivity has created a two-tier Indian gas generating fleet, with northeastern plants enjoying reliable domestic supply and high utilisation while western India benefits from proximity to LNG import terminals and developed infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Asset-level location determines value in Indian gas power — national averages are meaningless, screen by pipeline and terminal proximity.

insights.claim: Outside the favoured northeastern and western regions, limited fuel access severely depresses Indian gas plant utilisation rates.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Low-utilisation gas assets in unconnected regions are candidates for write-down or conversion, not for incremental LNG contracting.

themes.theme: Cost competition from renewables plus batteries

insights.claim: Declining renewable and battery costs are making renewable-plus-battery solutions increasingly competitive against Indian gas-fired generation, while persistently high and volatile LNG prices keep gas expensive.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: The flexibility niche gas hoped to occupy in India is being taken by storage before gas can scale — bearish for long-term Indian LNG-to-power demand assumptions.
insights.quote: Declining renewable and battery costs are making renewable-plus-battery solutions increasing competitive, while persistently high and volatile LNG prices make gas generation expensive.
insights.locator: 4. Pricing: Imported LNG is increasingly expensive

insights.claim: Most Indian gas-fired plants are only brought online during seasonal demand peaks when higher electricity prices make dispatch economically viable.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Indian gas-power LNG demand is spiky and seasonal, which argues for spot and short-term cargoes rather than long-term contracts.
insights.locator: 4. Pricing: Imported LNG is increasingly expensive
